In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of sulfation in the activation of hydroxylamine carcinogens and its relationship to the induction of tumors in liver and other organs.
the development of a carcinogen that is capable of inducing liver tumors in rats that are genetically deficient in sulfation.
the development of a new class of hepatocarcinogens that are metabolized in a manner different from that of the known carcinogenic arylamines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
partial hepatectopy and subsequent dietary phenobarbittal treatment are effective in the induction of liver neoplasia in female CD rats, whereas repeated partial hepatectomes are not.
the N-formyl derivative of N-hydrox-4-aminophenyl, in conjunction to partial hepatecty and phenobarbital-induced enzyme induction in the diet, is a weak hepatocarcinogen in the CD rat.
the N-hydroxy derivatives of 4-aminobenzoyl chloride and 4-acetamidobenzoylchloride are potent hepatocarcinogens and mammary carcinogens in female rats.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
N-hydroxy derivatives of arylamines are potent carcinogens and that the N-formyl group is a more efficient substituent than the acetyl group.
N-hydroxyarylamine derivatives can be potent liver carcinogens in the rat and that the carcinogenicity is enhanced by the induction of microsome enzyme activity and repeated partial hepatectomes.
the N-hydroxy group of arylhydroxylamines is the most critical part of the carcinogen for tumor induction in the liver and that the acyl group is of minor importance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
arylhydroxamates can be potent hepatocarcinogens, but that the presence of a sulfotransferasemediated activation pathway may be a prerequisite for their hepatocarcinogenesis in the rat.
the induction of liver tumorigenesis is not dependent on the activation of N-hydroxylated carcinogens by sulfotransferases.
partial hepatectory and phenobarbital administration are not necessary for the induction of liver neoplasia by N-hydroxyaroylaminobipenyls.
